My search tool stopped working partway through, so I only had excerpts of each page: sometimes the full verse note, sometimes just part of it. I found nothing from the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Pentecostal/Assemblies of God, NET Bible or Bible Odyssey sites, or on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Those sections are left out.

On Bible Hub's combined pages, some excerpts carry no commentator's name. I named them from the order the site always lists commentators in (Ellicott, Benson, Matthew Henry, Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Poole, Gill, Geneva). That is a reasoned guess, so check those names against the pages.

---

## Revelation 10: verse-by-verse notes

### v. 1: the mighty angel
- **Where this fits:** Chapter 9 ended with the sixth trumpet. Instead of the seventh trumpet, a pause follows that runs to 11:15. Guzik says the pause adds drama and also shows mercy, giving people more time to repent. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-10/
- **Comfort in the pause:** Such pauses reassure God's people in the middle of judgment that He is still in control and has not forgotten them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-10-commentary
- **The rainbow:** It recalls the flood in Noah's day. The judgments that follow are seen as parallel to the flood (compare Matthew 24:37–38). https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-10-commentary
- **The cloud and the rainbow:**
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the cloud stands for God coming in judgment. The rainbow stands for covenant mercy to His people while His enemies are judged, and points back to 4:3. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-1.htm
  - Barnes: the rainbow is a sign of peace. The angel comes on an errand of mercy, like sunshine after a storm. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-1.htm
  - Guzik: the rainbow recalls God's promise, and it is also what naturally appears when sun shines through cloud. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-10/
- **Who is the angel?** The traditional teachers disagree; see section 2 below.

### v. 2: the little scroll; feet on sea and land
- **The scroll:**
  - Guzik: John uses different words here than for the scroll of 5:1. The two are probably different but closely related. The little scroll may be a shorter version, the part John himself will see and write. He also cites Walvoord, who sees it as the written authority for the angel's mission. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-10/
  - Wesley: the little scroll holds the rest of the sealed scroll the Lamb opened. From here on, he says, Revelation speaks more plainly. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/revelation-10.html
- **The feet:**
  - Guzik, citing Walvoord and Clarke: the stance shows authority over the whole earth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-10/
  - Preceptaustin: the theme is God's right to take back the whole earth, land and sea. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-10-commentary
  - Wesley: the sea is where the first beast will rise (ch. 13) and the land where the second will rise. The sea may stand for Europe and the land for Asia. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/revelation-10.html
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: those beasts will rise only for a while, and their time will end. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Rev/Rev_010.cfm
- **Applied to Scripture:** S. Conway (Pulpit homilies) applies the planted feet to God's Word, which cannot be driven out. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/revelation-10.html

### v. 3: the lion's roar and the seven thunders
- **The thunders as God's voice:**
  - Guzik: links them to Psalm 29, where "the voice of the Lord" comes seven times. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-10/
  - GotQuestions: the Greek word means "to roar." Thunder often marks judgment in Scripture, and it stands for God's voice (Psalm 18:13). https://www.gotquestions.org/seven-thunders.html
- **The lion's roar:** Preceptaustin connects it to prophets who describe the LORD roaring like a lion in worldwide judgment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-10-commentary
- **Real words, not just noise:** Wesley: the thunders spoke clear words, one after another, through glorious heavenly powers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/revelation-10.html
- **Ellicott:** the lion-like voice is a sign that Christ, "the Lion of the tribe of Judah," is with the Church. He calls guesses about the thunders' content (for example, the seven Crusades) unlikely. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-3.htm

### v. 4: "Seal up… do not write it down"
- **A lesson in humility:** Guzik: God has secrets in His prophetic plan, which should keep our predictions humble. He cites Walvoord and Leon Morris. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-10/
- **Don't guess:**
  - GotQuestions: no reason is given (perhaps the content was too terrifying), so we should not guess. These are the only sealed words in Revelation. https://www.gotquestions.org/seven-thunders.html
  - Preceptaustin: guessing is pointless, though the context suggests the thunders concern the coming bowl judgments. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-10-commentary
- **Wesley:** the voice is "doubtless" Jesus Christ's. John learned something secret, and we are kept from asking what it was. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/revelation-10.html
- **Ellicott:** the thunders spoke real words that John could have written down. The message was for those who heard it, not for everyone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-4.htm
- **Poole:** forbidden because they concerned far-off events to be shown more fully later. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-4.htm
- **Gill:** John was to keep them in his own mind for now, because the same things would be shown again in another form. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-4.htm

### vv. 5–6: the oath; "no more delay"
- **The point of no return:** Guzik: the oath means the end is set in motion and cannot be turned back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-10/
- **Why God is named as Creator:**
  - Preceptaustin: the Creator owns what He made and is taking back the title to the earth. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-10-commentary
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the power that created all things can surely finish His plan. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-6.htm
- **"Delay," not "the end of time":**
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown links the verse to 6:11, where the martyrs were told to wait "a little longer." Now there is no more waiting. They reject the reading "time ends and eternity begins." They also note that Daniel's angel (Daniel 12:7) swore that a period of time would still pass, while this angel swears the waiting is over. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Rev/Rev_010.cfm
  - The Cambridge Bible and Gill agree that it means delay, not time giving way to eternity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-6.htm
  - Barnes notes that most scholars reject the old rendering "time no longer," because events continue after this. He lists other translations ("delay shall be no longer"; "the time shall not be yet"). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-6.htm
- **Matthew Henry** allows both readings, including one where, once the plan is finished, time itself is "swallowed up in eternity." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rev/Rev_010.cfm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** God's punishments were also chances to repent. That patience is now used up, so no more delay. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/revelation-10.html
- **Wesley:** of all the trumpets, only the seventh is backed by such an oath. The angel may be the same one as in Daniel 12:7. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/revelation-10.html

### v. 7: the mystery of God fulfilled
- **What mystery?**
  - Guzik lists New Testament uses of "mystery" (Israel's conversion, the Church, the Gentiles, Christ in the believer, the gospel). Here he takes it as God's plan for the ages being brought to its end. He suggests it may include the old question of why God allows rebellion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-10/
  - Preceptaustin gathers several views: MacArthur (God's plan fulfilled in Christ's kingdom); Henry Morris (why evil and suffering have been allowed); and the answer to the martyrs' "How long?" (6:10) and to "Thy kingdom come." It also stresses that the prophets faithfully wrote down what God told them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-10-commentary
- **Wesley:** the mystery is fulfilled when the dragon is removed, but only after God's wrath has been poured out in the bowls. The oath is meant to comfort believers who suffer. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/revelation-10.html

### vv. 8–9: "Take it and eat it"
- **Taking the scroll:** Some say "take it" shows God never forces His revelation on anyone. Guzik replies that this is often true, but not for Paul on the Damascus road. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-10/
- **Eating the scroll:**
  - Wesley: Ezekiel was given the same command. Eating stands for thinking it through and taking it in fully. The sweetness is the good that follows (11:15); the bitterness is the coming third woe. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/revelation-10.html
  - D. Thomas (Pulpit homilies): the gospel is not only for the mind or emotions but is to be taken in as food for the soul. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/revelation-10.html

### v. 10: sweet in the mouth, bitter in the stomach
- **Sweet:** Ellicott compares Ezekiel 3:3 and Psalms 19:10 and 119:103 (God's word sweeter than honey). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-10.htm
- **Why bitter:**
  - Matthew Henry: the sweetness is mixed with bitterness when we compare Scripture with the state of the world, the Church or our own hearts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-10.htm
  - Barnes: either the message of woe was painful to deliver, or receiving it brought persecution. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-10.htm
  - Poole: sweet as God's revelation, bitter because it was either hard to understand or sad. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-10.htm
  - Gill: preaching the gospel brings grief through persecution and hard hearts. The prophecy also showed John the suffering of the two witnesses (ch. 11). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-10.htm
  - Expositor's Bible Commentary: the bitterness can't come only from announcing judgment, since judgment rightly seen (as God putting things right) brings only joy. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/revelation-10.html
- **Applied:** Guzik's page summary says God's revelation is bittersweet because it shows both judgment and mercy, and that preachers must take in the Word deeply before speaking it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-10/
- **A devotional use (Seedbed, Wesleyan):** the writer applies the verse to their own "gut-level pain" when called to rejoice in God during hard times. https://seedbed.com/the-word-of-god-is-sweet-and-bitter-part-2/

### v. 11: "You must prophesy again"
- **The whole world:** Guzik's page summary says John's message is for the whole world, not just the Church. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-10/
- **Wesley:** John prophesies again about the mystery of God, starting with measuring the temple (11:1), since prophecy can be acted out as well as spoken. The "many kings" are kings who follow one another, linked to European kingdoms rising from the 8th century. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/revelation-10.html

---

## 2. Where traditions differ

Note that these differences run between individual teachers, often inside the same tradition, more than between whole traditions.

**Is the mighty angel Christ (v. 1, 5–6)?**
- **Christ:**
  - Matthew Henry (Presbyterian Nonconformist): probably our Lord, veiling His glory. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-1.htm
  - He also allows that the angel swore "by himself, as God often has done." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rev/Rev_010.cfm
  - Poole: the cloud and rainbow fit Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-1.htm
  - John Gill (Baptist): Christ appearing in vision to help His Church in dark times. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-1.htm
- **Undecided:**
  - Adam Clarke (Methodist): "Either Christ or his representative." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/revelation/10.htm
  - Ellicott (Anglican): the description seems to fit only Christ, but "another mighty angel" is a real difficulty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-1.htm
- **A created angel:**
  - John Wesley (Methodist): the angel swears by God, not by himself, and the glory is not too much for a creature (Matthew 13:43). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/revelation-10.html
  - The Cambridge Bible: the oath shows he is "in no sense a divine Person." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-6.htm
  - Coffman: Christ taking an oath would not fit; some have even named the angel as Gabriel or Martin Luther. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/revelation-10.html
  - Dispensational teachers: Keathley (Christ does not come down before the end of the Tribulation; possibly Michael) https://bible.org/seriespage/16-angel-and-little-book-rev-101-11; Preceptaustin (a non-divine messenger, because the Lamb stays in heaven until 19:11) https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-10-commentary
  - Guzik (Calvary Chapel; his site is on your Pentecostal/charismatic list): most likely Michael (Daniel 12). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-10/

**How the chapter is read overall (vv. 3–7)**
- **Reformation reading (older Protestants):**
  - Albert Barnes (Presbyterian) reads the angel as the Reformation, and the seven thunders as the Pope's condemnations ("papal thunders") from Rome, the seven-hilled city. He thinks John mistook them for real revelation and so was told not to write them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-3.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-4.htm
  - On v. 6 he notes that the Reformers (Luther, Melanchthon) widely expected the end soon. He reads the oath as "the time shall not be yet." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/revelation-10.html
  - Gill records Daubuz's view that the thunders were seven Protestant kingdoms, and that the sealing meant the Reformation would be stopped short. He also mentions a view that they were Reformation preachers, "sons of thunder." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-4.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-3.htm
  - Wesley, following Bengel, works out a timeline: a "non-chronos" running roughly from AD 800 to 1836. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/revelation-10.html
  - The Geneva Study Bible says the history of the Church begins here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-1.htm
- **Future reading (dispensational):** The thunders and the oath point to the bowl judgments of the future Tribulation and God's kingdom on earth. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-10-commentary and https://bible.org/seriespage/16-angel-and-little-book-rev-101-11
- **Timeless principles:** The Pulpit Commentary's homilies treat the open Bible of the Reformation as only one example, and read the chapter as truths that hold "for all time." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/revelation-10.html

---

## 3. Other views
- **Critical scholarship (v. 4):** A critical note on Bible Hub (citing German scholars) suggests the author is explaining why he left out a set of "seven thunders" visions already circulating among prophets of his day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/10-4.htm
- **An early Church voice (v. 1), reported second-hand:** A Bible Hub article says Victorinus (c. AD 280) called the angel "one of the chief angels." https://biblehub.com/q/Who_is_the_mighty_angel_in_Rev_10_1.htm
- **Christian Science (v. 2):** Mary Baker Eddy claimed the little scroll was Christian Science. Norman Geisler, quoted on Preceptaustin, answers that the text contains no Christian Science teaching and that the scroll made John sick rather than healing him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-10-commentary
